candidates.attacker_control: A network peer able to send an AJP forward request can control the request URI, headers, and arbitrary request-attribute names and string values, including the javax.servlet.include.* attributes. The shipped AJP connector is enabled on port 8009 without a required secret or localhost-only bind address.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Verified that the AJP processor has no attribute allowlist and no default secret, and that the shipped server.xml does not set requiredSecret. Verified that Request.getAttribute exposes Coyote attributes to DefaultServlet. Checked StandardRoot path validation: it blocks ../ escaping from the web application, so the claim is limited to files under the web application resource root, not arbitrary filesystem access. Checked that an explicitly configured requiredSecret would cause missing or incorrect secrets to be rejected. No runtime test or exploit was performed.
candidates.impact: Unauthenticated disclosure of files under a deployed web application's resource root, especially WEB-INF/web.xml, context descriptors, classes, and application configuration that may contain secrets. It can become a code-execution chain only where another capability lets the attacker place a crafted file in the web application; that additional condition is not established by this source alone.
candidates.prerequisites: The AJP connector must be reachable from the attacker (not firewalled or restricted to a trusted proxy), the target web application must use the default servlet, and the requested file must be readable under that application's resource root. A configured requiredSecret, connector address restriction, or network isolation mitigates the path.
candidates.root_cause: The AJP connector accepts arbitrary SC_A_REQ_ATTRIBUTE name/value pairs and stores them on the request. Its requiredSecret is null by default, and the shipped server.xml enables the AJP connector without configuring one. The default servlet then treats attacker-supplied javax.servlet.include.request_uri/servlet_path/path_info attributes as authoritative when calculating the web resource path, rather than verifying that an actual container include created them.
candidates.title: Unauthenticated AJP request-attribute injection can expose WEB-INF content through DefaultServlet
candidates.trace: An AJP forward request supplies SC_A_REQ_ATTRIBUTE entries such as javax.servlet.include.request_uri, javax.servlet.include.servlet_path, and javax.servlet.include.path_info. prepareRequest stores them verbatim in the Coyote request; because requiredSecret is null, the secret check at the end of attribute processing is skipped. Request.getAttribute falls through to the Coyote attribute map. The request URI is mapped normally to DefaultServlet, which sees the injected include.request_uri and builds its resource path from the injected servlet_path/path_info. resources.getResource resolves the resulting /WEB-INF/... path and serveResource writes the readable file to the response.
candidates.unverified: Whether AJP port 8009 is reachable in a particular deployment, whether firewalling or connector address binding prevents access, which web applications and files are present, and whether any upload-to-webroot capability exists. The finding is a static lead, not a runtime-confirmed vulnerability.
candidates.weakness_type: Missing authentication for an exposed protocol path leading to external control of a resource path (CWE-306/CWE-73)

coverage_summary: Source scope reports 2,799 model-visible source files, with no over-5-MiB, sensitive-name, or symlink exclusions; binary-like files are refused or skipped when a NUL byte is detected. The P1 relation index covers the same 2,799 files with no missing files and reports complete indexing, but it is syntactic navigation only and provides no complete data-flow, reachability, or exploitability proof. I reviewed the shipped server/web configuration, AJP connector/processor, connector request attribute handling, default servlet resource resolution, URI normalization, HTTP/1.1 parsing, HTTP/2 handling, authentication/form handling, realms, CGI, and session-related paths. No builds, tests, scanners, runtime checks, or exploit payloads were executed.
limitations: Static source review only; no runtime deployment, network reachability, authentication state, or exploitability was verified.
AJP exposure depends on deployment topology and firewall/address-binding choices even though the shipped configuration enables port 8009 without a secret.
The file disclosure is limited by StandardRoot's normalization to resources under the selected web application; arbitrary host filesystem access was not established.
Any code-execution consequence is conditional on a separate attacker-controlled write/upload capability and was not demonstrated.
The relation index is navigation-only and cannot prove actual call paths, data flow, or reachability.
The review was broad but not a line-by-line audit of every one of the 2,799 files; other configuration-dependent issues may remain.

rejected_leads.lead: HTTP/1.1 Transfer-Encoding/Content-Length request smuggling in Http11Processor
rejected_leads.reason: The parser is old and parses only one transfer-encoding value, but exploitation depends on a front-end proxy's differing interpretation and was not demonstrated from this source. It is less direct than the AJP/default-servlet path.

rejected_leads.lead: CGI command-line argument injection in CGIServlet
rejected_leads.reason: The decoded and encoded argument patterns are present, the servlet is not mapped by default, and no bypass was established. This was not selected.

rejected_leads.lead: Persistent session deserialization or FileStore path issues
rejected_leads.reason: Requires a non-default persistent manager plus attacker-controlled session files or an upload/write primitive; it is not a directly reachable default path.
Configuration-dependent LDAP filter construction may be injectable, but authentication still depends on configured credentials and directory behavior; no concrete bypass was established.

summary: The strongest source-supported lead is an unauthenticated AJP request-attribute path that can make the default servlet disclose files under a deployed web application, including WEB-INF content. The shipped configuration enables the AJP connector on port 8009 without a required secret; the AJP processor accepts attacker-named request attributes and the default servlet trusts the servlet/include attributes when constructing its resource path. This is a source-level lead only, not a runtime-confirmed exploit.
